newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Truckers' strikes widen in French Guiana.
newsitem.headline: Truckers' strikes widen in French Guiana.

text.p: A truckers' strike paralysing French Guiana widened on Saturday as other local businesses joined the protests to push for government aid to combat recession.

The truckers' strike, which began on Wednesday, is blocking fuel distribution in the French overseas department, forcing petrol stations to close for lack of fuel. Roads to the main port, near the capital Cayenne, were blocked, witnesses said.

Other groups, including shopkeepers, fishermen and construction firms, joined the strikes on Saturday with demands such as tax breaks, cuts in payroll charges and talks on the economic crisis with Prime Minister Alain Juppe in Paris.
Representatives of the strikers threatened to widen their action with an air and sea blockage of French Guiana if the demands were not met.
The French overseas department on the northeast coast of South America has been rocked by strikes and riots for the last six months amid a worsening economic crisis.
Activity from the European Space Agency (ESA) Ariane rocket launch centre in Kourou represents over half of all economic activity, but is not expected to bring any growth in coming years.
The Paris-based Arianespace company controls more than half the world's commercial rocket launch market. It successfully launched 15 satellites aboard 10 Ariane-4 rockets in 1996.

French Guiana has been in French hands since the 17th century and is the only non-independent territory on the continent. In 1946, Paris granted Guiana the status of a "department" giving it official equality with mainland France.

"The entire economic and social system that is tied to 1946's status of department is crumbling completely and suffocating all small and medium sized enterprises," said Alex Weimert, a member of French Guiana's Chamber of Commerce.
"At the same time space activity is more and more active; more and more disconnected with the rest of (French) Guiana society," Weimart told a news conference.

French Guiana lags behind mainland France in housing, education and health. Official unemployment exceeds 23 percent and young people under 25, who make up half of the population, are hardest hit. Thousands of youths are not attending school.

Illegal immigrants, mostly from Haiti, Brazil and neighbouring Surinam, represent an estimated 25 percent of the population of 150,000. More than 8,000 of the total population receive French welfare payments.
